title: RS Encoder Lab — Parity as a Remainder (GSM/EDGE RS8(85,73))

questions.question: In a polynomial-view Reed–Solomon code, what makes a codeword “valid”?
options: It has an even number of 1 bits.
It is divisible by the generator polynomial g(x) over the field.
It has a checksum byte equal to 0x00.
It decodes correctly for any number of errors.
questions.explanation: In the cyclic/polynomial view, valid codewords are exactly the multiples of g(x), so dividing by g(x) leaves remainder 0.

questions.question: In GF(2^8) as used in this lesson, what is addition?
options: Integer addition modulo 256.
Bitwise XOR.
Carryless multiplication reduced mod the primitive polynomial.
Lookup in a log table.
questions.explanation: GF(2^m) addition is coefficient-wise mod 2, which is XOR on bytes.

questions.question: For the GSM/EDGE RS8(255,243) code in this lesson, what is the first consecutive root exponent (first_root / B) used to build g(x)?
questions.explanation: GSM/EDGE uses g(x) = ∏_{i=0}^{11} (x − α^{i+122}), which makes the listed coefficients self-reciprocal.

questions.question: Systematic RS encoding computes parity symbols as the remainder of which division?
options: remainder[D(x) / g(x)]
remainder[x^nsym · D(x) / g(x)]
remainder[g(x) / D(x)]
remainder[D(x) / x^nsym]
questions.explanation: You multiply the message polynomial by x^nsym (append nsym zeros) and take the remainder modulo g(x); that remainder becomes parity.

questions.question: How do you shorten RS(255,243) to RS(85,73) in the method used here?
options: Append 170 zeros to the codeword after encoding, then truncate parity.
Prepend 170 zeros to the message to make 243 symbols, encode as RS(255,243), then drop the first 170 codeword symbols.
Append 170 zeros to the message to make 243 symbols, encode, then drop the last 170 codeword symbols.
Encode 73 symbols directly with the same generator polynomial without any padding.
questions.explanation: Shortening is done by inserting known-zero symbols into the message (here: 170 leading zeros), encoding at full length, then removing the corresponding leading codeword symbols.

questions.question: What does it usually mean if the syndromes at the generator roots are not all zero?
options: The codeword is valid and error-free.
The codeword is not a multiple of g(x) (so it is corrupted or from a different RS convention).
The primitive polynomial must be 0x11B.
The message length is always too long.
questions.explanation: Non-zero syndromes indicate the received polynomial is not divisible by g(x), which means an error or a convention mismatch.

questions.question: Why can two encoders with the same (n,k) and the same GF(256) primitive polynomial still be incompatible?
options: Because XOR is not associative.
Because the first consecutive root (first_root / B) and symbol ordering conventions can differ, changing g(x) and parity.
Because g(x) is unique for any (n,k).
Because systematic encoding is impossible in GF(256).
questions.explanation: The generator polynomial depends on the chosen root set (including B), and implementations can also disagree on symbol order; both affect parity and interop.

questions.question: If an encoder claims it is systematic, which property must hold for its output codeword?
options: The parity symbols come first, then the message.
The codeword has no zero symbols.
The first k symbols of the codeword equal the original message symbols exactly.
The syndromes are random-looking but small.
questions.explanation: Systematic encoding preserves the message symbols verbatim in the codeword and appends parity symbols.
